---
title: "11. Price your own claim"
aliases:
  - /price-your-own-claim.html
---

Everything in this course so far priced the paper's three claims: the market and
the two legs of the book-to-market sort. This chapter shows you how to
price a claim of your own: a portfolio's dividends, a firm's
distributable earnings, or any cash-flow stream you can put a growth
series to. The model reports how the claim's valuation responds
to long-run growth news and what that exposure costs.

The contrast to remember is [Chapter 1](01-two-free-numbers.qmd). A DCF
prices a claim from two free numbers, a growth rate and a discount rate,
and nothing inside the method disciplines either one. Here the claim
brings exactly one number, the loading of its cash flows on the
persistent component of consumption growth, measured from cash flows
alone. Nobody chooses the discount rate: the household of
[Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) sets it and prices every
claim in the cross-section from one economy and one set of preferences.
Returns never enter the estimation, so the premium that comes out is a
prediction, not a fit.

## The steps

Pricing a claim takes four steps, and none of them uses a return.

1. **Obtain your claim's cash-flow growth series.** Use annual log
   dividend growth for a portfolio, or growth in distributable
   earnings for a firm; it is the only input the claim contributes.
2. **Measure its long-run leverage.** Project the growth series on the
   two-year moving average of lagged consumption growth, as in equation
   (19) of the paper and
   [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd). The slope is the loading
   $\tilde\phi$.
3. **Build a claim from the loading, put it in a model, and solve.**
   `lrr.ClaimParams.from_loading(phi)` describes the claim, and
   `lrr.LongRunRisksModel(claims={"claim": ...})` puts it in the Table
   II economy. `.solve(method="analytical")` solves the log-linear
   model of [Chapter 6](06-log-linear-solution.qmd) for that one claim.
   A single-claim model has no market claim to measure against, so
   market betas are undefined and the analytical method is the one to
   use.
4. **Read off the outputs.** `A1` is the elasticity of the
   price-dividend ratio to $x_t$, so it measures how the claim's
   valuation responds to growth news. `long_run_premium` is the
   annualized compensation for bearing that news, in percent.
   `gordon_return` is what a Gordon growth formula would report at the
   same anchor, using the growth channel alone with no adjustment for
   risk.

## Two synthetic firms

Before using real data, run the cleanest possible experiment: price two
firms identical in every respect except the loading, with nothing
estimated and nothing re-tuned between the rows. Both firms go into
one model, so a single solve prices the pair and the code shows the
one field that changes between them.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
# Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this
# notebook runs outside the repository.
from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request

DATA = Path("../../data")
if not DATA.exists():
    DATA = Path("data")
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/"
            "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/")
    for f in ("annual_panel.csv", "consumption_annual.csv", "rf_annual.csv"):
        if not (DATA / f).exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f)
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import lrrcs as lrr
from great_tables import GT

KIKU_GT = dict(table_background_color="transparent",
               table_font_size="0.92rem",
               heading_title_font_size="1.05rem",
               heading_subtitle_font_size="0.85rem",
               source_notes_font_size="0.8rem",
               column_labels_font_weight="bold",
               data_row_padding="4px")

# Everything a claim needs beyond its loading, held fixed across the firms.
BASE = dict(mu=0.0015, phi_sigma=7.5, alpha=0.5)

firms = lrr.LongRunRisksModel(
    claims={"A": dict(BASE, phi=0.5), "B": dict(BASE, phi=1.5)},
).solve(method="analytical")

names = list(firms.claims)
rows = pd.DataFrame({
    "firm": names,
    "phi": [firms.params.claims[n].phi for n in names],
    "a1": [firms.A1[n] for n in names],
    "prem": [firms.long_run_premium[n] for n in names],
    "growth": [firms.expected_growth[n] for n in names],
    "gordon": [firms.gordon_return[n] for n in names],
})

(
    GT(rows)
    .tab_header(title="Two firms that differ only in the loading")
    .cols_label(firm="firm", phi="phi", a1="A1", prem="long_run_premium %",
                growth="expected_growth %", gordon="gordon_return %")
    .fmt_number(columns="phi", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns="a1", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns=["prem", "growth", "gordon"], decimals=2)
    .tab_source_note("One analytical solve of a two-claim model on the "
                     "Table II economy.")
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

Firm B's dividends track the persistent component of consumption, so
its valuation moves with long-run news ($A_1 = 15.2$) and earns a
positive premium, 0.14 percent a year. Firm A's loading of 0.5
sits below the household's $1/\psi = 0.67$ threshold from
[Chapter 6](06-log-linear-solution.qmd), so its valuation moves against
the news instead ($A_1 = -3.0$) and earns a slightly negative premium,
$-0.03$ percent. A hedge pays less, because the household accepts a
lower return on a claim that does well precisely when long-run news is
bad.

The Gordon column uses only expected growth, so it puts the two firms
0.12 points apart (7.01 versus 6.89 percent), which is almost entirely
the mechanical growth difference. The economics is in the risk Gordon
omits: `long_run_premium` is the part from $x_t$ news, and short-run
and volatility news add more.

## Pricing the value and growth legs

Now run the same steps on the 1930 to 2003 data that
[Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) built. The value leg is
missing dividend growth in two depression years, so the regression
masks non-finite pairs, the same arithmetic Chapter 8 ran:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

dc = pl.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv").sort("year")["dc"].to_numpy()
panel = pl.read_csv(DATA / "annual_panel.csv")

def dividend_growth(claim):
    return (
        panel.filter(pl.col("claim") == claim)
        .sort("year")["dgrowth"]
        .to_numpy()
    )

ma = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(dc, window=2)

def leverage(dd):
    mask = np.isfinite(ma) & np.isfinite(dd)
    x = ma[mask] - ma[mask].mean()
    e = dd[mask] - dd[mask].mean()
    return float(np.dot(x, e) / np.dot(x, x))

phi = {c: leverage(dividend_growth(c)) for c in ("Value", "Growth", "Market")}
(
    GT(pd.DataFrame({"claim": list(phi), "slope": list(phi.values())}))
    .tab_header(title="Measured long-run leverages")
    .cols_label(claim="", slope="phi_tilde")
    .fmt_number(columns="slope", decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

Value's dividends load heavily on the slow component of consumption,
and growth's barely respond; on the reconstruction here, growth's
slope is even slightly negative. For complete series,
`lrr.calibrate_claims` also estimates the short-run parameters
($\mu$, $\phi_\sigma$, $\alpha$) from one growth series per claim,
returning them under the name you gave each:

```{python}
div = lrr.calibrate_claims(
    dc,
    {"Growth": dividend_growth("Growth"),
     "Market": dividend_growth("Market")},
    frequency="annual",
    window=2,
)
(
    GT(pd.DataFrame([
        {"portfolio": name, "mu": d.mu, "phi": d.phi,
         "phi_sigma": d.phi_sigma, "alpha": d.alpha}
        for name, d in div.items()
    ]))
    .tab_header(title="Calibrated claim parameters")
    .cols_label(portfolio="", mu="mu (monthly)", phi="phi (long-run)",
                phi_sigma="phi_sigma", alpha="alpha")
    .fmt_number(columns="mu", decimals=5)
    .fmt_number(columns="phi", decimals=3)
    .fmt_number(columns=["phi_sigma", "alpha"], decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

The slopes match the regression above, and the signature takes no
argument for returns, so the Euler equation stays a test, not a
target.

Steps 3 and 4 put both measured loadings into one model, held at the
same values as the two synthetic firms above. The `compare` call below
picks which pair of priced claims makes a spread worth reporting, for
any pair you name:

```{python}
legs = lrr.LongRunRisksModel(
    claims={"value leg": dict(BASE, phi=phi["Value"]),
            "growth leg": dict(BASE, phi=phi["Growth"])},
).solve(method="analytical")

spread = legs.compare("value leg", "growth leg")
print(f"Value-growth spread from long-run risks: "
      f"{spread.premium:.2f} points")

leg_names = list(legs.claims)
(
    GT(pd.DataFrame({
        "leg": leg_names,
        "phi": [legs.params.claims[n].phi for n in leg_names],
        "a1": [legs.A1[n] for n in leg_names],
        "prem": [legs.long_run_premium[n] for n in leg_names],
    }))
    .tab_header(title="The two legs priced from measured loadings")
    .cols_label(leg="", phi="phi", a1="A1", prem="long_run_premium %")
    .fmt_number(columns="phi", decimals=2)
    .fmt_number(columns="a1", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns="prem", decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

The premium ordering follows the measured leverage. The leg whose
dividends load on long-run news earns compensation for that risk, and
the leg whose dividends do not earns a small hedge discount, though no
return entered the calculation.

Seventy annual observations establish a ranking, not a third decimal.
Table VI of the paper reports annual slopes of $-0.38$ for growth and
$2.16$ for value, where the reconstruction here prints $-0.27$ and
$12.13$, so the ranking survives and the point estimates do not. An
annual slope is also not the monthly loading the full solution uses
(Table II sets $\phi_V = 6.2$, $\phi_G = 2.6$), and at
$\tilde\phi = 12.13$ the log-linear elasticity of 208.9 comes from
applying the formula well past the region it was linearized for.

## When your claim is not a traded portfolio

The steps do not require a traded portfolio, since any cash-flow
growth series can be projected on the consumption moving average.
Measurement error and the linearization anchor still deserve extra
caution outside one.

First, the loading is measured with error: seven decades of
exchange-listed dividends still moved the point estimate from 2.16 to
12.13 across reconstructions. A firm's distributable earnings over 15
or 20 years measure $\tilde\phi$ with even more error, so price it at
the low and high ends of a confidence band, not at the point
estimate.

Second, the anchor is an assumption: a claim with no anchor in the
model linearizes around a mean log price-dividend ratio of 3.30, and
`mean_log_pd` repeats that assumption rather than predicting your
claim's actual valuation. If your valuation ratio sits far from
$e^{3.30} \approx 27$, the elasticities and the Gordon comparison
drift with it, so move the anchor by passing `pd_anchor=` to `solve`.
The sign and ordering logic survives: a loading above $1/\psi$ earns
a premium for good long-run news, and a loading below it earns the
opposite.

## Takeaways

- Any claim is priced from one measured number, the loading of its
  cash-flow growth on the two-year moving average of consumption
  growth, and returns never enter, so the premium is a prediction.
- The analytical solve returns three numbers: the valuation response to
  growth news (`A1`), the compensation it commands
  (`long_run_premium`), and the Gordon return a DCF would report
  instead.
- A loading above $1/\psi$ earns a premium for growth-news risk, and a
  loading below it earns a small hedge discount.
- On the 1930 to 2003 data the measured leverages order value above
  growth, and the implied premium ordering follows.
- Outside a traded portfolio the loading is measured with error and the
  linearization anchor is an assumption, so trust the ordering and the
  sign, not the third decimal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check yourself"}

Answer from memory, then open the answers.

1. Price a claim with $\phi = 1/\psi$, the household's loading.
   Explain why that threshold, not zero, is where `A1` and
   `long_run_premium` cross zero.
2. Re-run the equation (19) regression with `window=3` in
   `expected_growth_proxy`. Does the value-growth leverage ranking
   survive?
3. Drop 1930 to 1945 from the sample and re-estimate $\tilde\phi$ for
   both legs. How much does the spread move, and which years carry the
   identifying variation?

**Answers.**

1. At $\phi = 1/\psi$ the claim's dividends grow with expected
   consumption, so the elasticity and the premium both go to zero. The
   threshold is $1/\psi$ because that is the growth rate the household
   expects.
2. No. At window 3 the value slope turns negative, the same instability
   the Chapter 8 check found, so trust no single-window estimate at
   face value.
3. The pre-war years carry most of the identifying variation, so the
   post-war slopes and the value-growth spread shrink once 1930 to 1945
   drops out.

   ```{python}
   #| code-fold: true
   # Exercise 1: the riskless long-run loading
   res0 = lrr.LongRunRisksModel(
       claims={"claim": lrr.ClaimParams.from_loading(1 / 1.5)}
   ).solve(method="analytical")
   print(f"phi = 1/psi = {1/1.5:.3f}:  A1 = {res0.A1['claim']:.3f}, "
         f"long-run premium = {res0.long_run_premium['claim']:+.3f} %/yr")

   # Exercise 2: a different proxy window
   ma3 = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(dc, window=3)
   def leverage_on(dd, proxy):
       mask = np.isfinite(proxy) & np.isfinite(dd)
       x = proxy[mask] - proxy[mask].mean()
       e = dd[mask] - dd[mask].mean()
       return float(np.dot(x, e) / np.dot(x, x))
   for c in ("Value", "Growth"):
       print(f"{c:6s}  window 2: {phi[c]:7.2f}"
             f"   window 3: {leverage_on(dividend_growth(c), ma3):7.2f}")

   # Exercise 3: dropping 1930-1945
   years_c = (pl.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv").sort("year")
              ["year"].to_numpy())
   keep = years_c >= 1946
   ma_post = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(dc[keep], window=2)
   lev = {}
   for c in ("Value", "Growth"):
       dd_post = (panel.filter(pl.col("claim") == c)
                  .filter(pl.col("year") >= 1946).sort("year")
                  ["dgrowth"].to_numpy())
       lev[c] = leverage_on(dd_post, ma_post)
   post = lrr.LongRunRisksModel(
       claims={c: lrr.ClaimParams.from_loading(lev[c]) for c in lev}
   ).solve(method="analytical")
   for c in ("Value", "Growth"):
       print(f"{c:6s}  post-war phi: {lev[c]:7.2f}   "
             f"premium: {post.long_run_premium[c]:+.2f} %/yr")
   print(f"post-war spread: "
         f"{post.compare('Value', 'Growth').premium:.2f} points")
   ```
